questions.stem: On a hot day, a person drinks very little water and sweats heavily. What changes would you expect in their urine?

options.text: Large volume of dilute, pale urine
Small volume of concentrated, dark yellow urine
Normal volume of urine with no colour change
No urine production at all

questions.explanation: When dehydrated, the body conserves water. The pituitary gland releases more ADH, which makes the collecting ducts more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed back into the blood. This results in a small volume of concentrated, dark urine.

questions.stem: A patient's blood is tested and found to have a higher than normal water potential (too dilute). How would the body respond to restore normal blood concentration?

options.text: The pituitary gland releases more ADH, making the kidneys reabsorb more water
The pituitary gland releases less ADH, so less water is reabsorbed and more dilute urine is produced
The adrenal glands release adrenaline to increase blood pressure
The liver converts excess water into glycogen for storage

questions.explanation: When blood is too dilute (high water potential), the pituitary gland releases less ADH. This makes the collecting ducts less permeable to water, so less water is reabsorbed and more dilute urine is produced, restoring blood concentration to normal. This is negative feedback.

questions.stem: ADH (antidiuretic hormone) acts on the collecting ducts of the nephron. What is the specific effect of ADH on these structures?

options.text: ADH causes the collecting ducts to actively pump water into the urine
ADH increases the permeability of the collecting duct walls, allowing more water to be reabsorbed by osmosis
ADH blocks the collecting ducts so no urine can pass through
ADH breaks down urea in the collecting duct to release water

questions.explanation: ADH makes the walls of the collecting ducts more permeable to water by inserting aquaporin channels. This allows more water to leave the collecting duct by osmosis (moving into the surrounding medulla tissue and back into the blood), producing more concentrated urine.

questions.stem: A person with diabetes insipidus produces very little ADH. What symptom would you most expect them to experience?

options.text: High blood glucose levels
Production of large volumes of very dilute urine and extreme thirst
Dark concentrated urine and low thirst
Protein in the urine due to kidney damage

questions.explanation: Without ADH, the collecting ducts remain impermeable to water, so very little water is reabsorbed. The patient produces large volumes of dilute urine (up to 20 litres per day) and becomes severely dehydrated, causing extreme thirst. This is different from diabetes mellitus.

questions.stem: Alcohol inhibits the release of ADH from the pituitary gland. Using your knowledge of water balance, why do people who drink alcohol often become dehydrated?

options.text: Alcohol directly damages the kidneys, preventing all filtration
With less ADH, the collecting ducts reabsorb less water, leading to large volumes of dilute urine and net water loss
Alcohol increases ADH, causing the body to retain too much water
Alcohol replaces water in the blood plasma

questions.explanation: Alcohol suppresses ADH release. Without ADH, the collecting ducts become less permeable to water, so more water passes into the urine instead of being reabsorbed. This increases urine volume and leads to dehydration, explaining the thirst associated with alcohol consumption.
